Babylon the Great
BAB-ih-lon the grayt
noun phrase (Revelation 17-18)
From Babylon, the ancient city of pride and idolatry, taken up in the Revelation as the symbolic name of the great harlot-city opposed to God and His people.

Biblical Definition

Babylon the Great is the symbolic name given in the Revelation to the great harlot-city that embodies the world-system in its pride, idolatry, luxury, and hatred of the people of God. Upon her forehead is written, “MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.” She sits upon many waters and upon a beast; she is drunken with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus; she is the seat of the world's commerce, seduction, and false worship. Her doom is certain: an angel cries mightily, “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen,” and a voice from heaven summons God's people, “Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues.” The dictionary follows the historic Protestant and Reformed reading that sees in Babylon, beyond the literal ancient city, the great enemy-system of every age—the world in its organized rebellion against God—and, in the Reformers' particular application, the corrupt and persecuting power of false religion seated in a great city. Interpreters differ over the precise referent (apostate Rome, the persecuting world-empire, the final manifestation of antichristian power), and the dictionary does not bind the conscience to a single identification. What is certain is the moral meaning: Babylon is the city of man set against the city of God, glorious and seductive in her luxuries, bloody in her persecutions, and appointed to fall. The summons to the saints is the abiding application: come out of her, be not partakers of her sins, set your hope on the city that hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.

Webster 1828 Definition

The symbolic harlot-city of Revelation 17-18 embodying the world-system in pride, idolatry, luxury, and persecution; drunken with the blood of the saints and appointed to fall, with the summons, “Come out of her, my people.”

BABYLON THE GREAT, noun phrase. The symbolic harlot-city of the Revelation, the world-system opposed to God.

“MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS” (Revelation 17:5).

Drunken with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus (Revelation 17:6).

Her doom: “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen” (Revelation 18:2).

The summons: “Come out of her, my people” (Revelation 18:4).

Key Scripture

Re 17:5 — "And upon her forehead was a name written, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH."

Re 18:2 — "And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird."

Re 18:4 — "And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues."

Re 17:6 — "And I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus: and when I saw her, I wondered with great admiration."

Modern Corruption

The sensational date-setting school turns Babylon into a coded prediction of current events and headlines, while the spiritualizing school empties her of all reference to real, judgable evil.

expand to see more

One corruption, found in much popular prophecy teaching, reduces Babylon the Great to a cipher for the latest headline—a particular nation, a coming world government, a rebuilt city—and reads the Revelation as a coded almanac of current events. The dictionary counsels sobriety. The Spirit gave Babylon as a moral and theological symbol of the world-system in its pride, idolatry, and persecution; she has worn many faces through history, and interpreters may reasonably differ on her precise referent without making the text a newspaper to be decoded afresh each decade.

The opposite corruption spiritualizes Babylon into a vague principle with no real referent and no real judgment, so that the summons “come out of her” loses its edge. But Babylon is no abstraction: she is drunken with the blood of the martyrs, and her fall is the vindication of the saints she slew. The dictionary holds the historic Protestant reading that sees in her the organized worldly and false-religious power opposed to Christ, and presses the abiding application: God's people are summoned to separate from her sins, to refuse her luxuries and her idolatries, and to set their hope on the city of God that shall stand when Babylon is fallen.

Hebrew Roots

From Babylon (Hebrew Babel, “confusion”), the ancient city of pride and idolatry, taken into the Revelation as the type of the world-system; “mystery” (Greek mysterion) marks the name as symbolic.

expand to see more

Babel, Hebrew, “confusion,” the city of the tower and the type of human pride against God.

Mysterion, Greek, “mystery,” marking “Babylon” here as a symbolic name.

Porne, Greek, harlot, the figure of the seductive, idolatrous world-city.

“Drunken with the blood of the saints” names her as the persecutor of the church.

“Come out of her” echoes the call to flee literal Babylon (Jeremiah 51:45).

Usage

"The pastor preached Babylon the Great as the world-system in its pride and persecution, summoning the saints to come out of her."

"He warned against decoding Babylon as the day's headlines, reading her instead as the Spirit gave her."

"She set her hope on the city of God, refusing the luxuries and idolatries of fallen Babylon."
